summary: Moses expresses doubts about his mission to Pharaoh and the Israelites (vv. 1, 10, 13). God gives Moses three miraculous signs to convince the people (vv. 2-9) and appoints Aaron, Moses' brother, to speak for him (vv. 14-16). God then instructs Moses to return to Egypt, warning him that Pharaoh's heart will be hardened and that God will kill Pharaoh's firstborn if he refuses to let Israel go (vv. 19-23). During the journey, God attempts to kill Moses, but Zipporah saves him by circumcising their son (vv. 24-26). Finally, Moses and Aaron meet, gather the Israelite elders, perform the signs, and the people believe and worship God (vv. 27-31).
setting: The events begin in Midian, where Moses has been living (v. 19). Moses then travels back towards Egypt (v. 20), stopping at an inn along the way (v. 24). Aaron meets Moses in the desert, at 'the mountain of God' (v. 27). The wider situation is that God has called Moses to lead the Israelites out of slavery in Egypt.

events.what: Moses tells God that the Israelites will not believe him.
God gives Moses three signs to perform: his rod turning into a serpent and back, his hand becoming leprous and healing, and river water turning into blood. These are to convince the Israelites.
Moses again objects, saying he is not eloquent, and asks God to send someone else.
God becomes angry and appoints Aaron, Moses' brother, to speak for Moses to the people and Pharaoh. Moses is to put God's words in Aaron's mouth and keep the rod for signs.
God tells Moses to return to Egypt because those who sought his life are dead. Moses takes his family and the rod and begins the journey.

God instructs Moses to perform wonders before Pharaoh and warns that God will harden Pharaoh's heart. Moses is to tell Pharaoh that if he does not let Israel, God's firstborn, go, God will kill Pharaoh's firstborn.
At an inn, God attempts to kill Moses. Zipporah circumcises her son, touches Moses' feet with the foreskin, and God lets Moses go.
God tells Aaron to meet Moses. They meet in the desert, and Moses tells Aaron all of God's words and commands.
Moses and Aaron gather the elders of Israel. Aaron speaks God's words, and Moses performs the signs. The people believe and worship.

people.name: Moses
people.role: The chosen leader who expresses doubts and receives instructions and miraculous powers from God.

people.name: Lord
people.role: God, who speaks to Moses, gives him commands, performs signs, and expresses anger.

people.name: Aaron
people.role: Moses' brother, appointed by God to be Moses' spokesman to the people and Pharaoh.

people.name: Sephora
people.role: Moses' wife, who circumcises her son to save Moses' life.

people.name: Pharao
people.role: The ruler of Egypt, who God says will have a hardened heart and whose firstborn will be killed.

people.name: Israelites
people.role: The people whom Moses is sent to lead out of Egypt, who are to believe the signs and worship God.

people.name: ancients of the children of Israel
people.role: Elders of the Israelite community who are assembled to hear God's message.

people.name: sons
people.role: Moses' children, one of whom is circumcised by Zipporah.

terms.meaning: A staff or stick, used by Moses, which God uses to perform signs (vv. 2-4, 17, 20).
A skin condition, described as white like snow, which God causes and then heals on Moses' hand (v. 6).
Able to speak clearly and persuasively (v. 10). Moses claims he is not eloquent.
To make someone stubborn or resistant to persuasion (v. 21). God states He will do this to Pharaoh.
The eldest child (v. 22). God refers to Israel as His firstborn and threatens to kill Pharaoh's firstborn.
A place of lodging for travelers (v. 24).
The cutting off of the foreskin, a ritual practice (v. 25).
A phrase used by Zipporah after circumcising her son (v. 25). The exact meaning is debated, but it is linked to the act of circumcision.

readings.view: Often emphasizes Moses' humility and reluctance as a mark of true leadership, and God's patience in addressing his concerns (vv. 10-13). The incident at the inn (vv. 24-26) is sometimes seen as a reminder of the importance of the covenant of circumcision, even for leaders.

Often views Moses' reluctance as a human struggle with a divine calling, which God overcomes by providing assistance (Aaron) and miraculous power (signs). The hardening of Pharaoh's heart (v. 21) is frequently discussed in relation to divine sovereignty and human free will.

Focuses on the literary structure and potential sources of the text. The incident at the inn (vv. 24-26) is often considered a distinct narrative unit, possibly reflecting an ancient etiology or a separate tradition about the importance of circumcision, which was later integrated into the larger Moses narrative. The repeated objections of Moses (vv. 1, 10, 13) are sometimes seen as a literary device to highlight God's power and determination.

While Moses (Musa) is a highly revered prophet, the specific details of this chapter, particularly the incident at the inn (vv. 24-26), are not typically found in the Quran or prominent Islamic narratives, which focus more on Moses' direct encounters with Pharaoh and the miracles God performed through him.

oftenQuoted.caution: This verse, 'Who made man's mouth? or who made the dumb and the deaf, the seeing and the blind? did not I?', is often quoted to emphasize God's sovereignty over human abilities. In its context, it is God's direct response to Moses' claim of not being eloquent, reassuring Moses that God will enable him to speak.

The phrase 'I shall harden his heart' is frequently cited in discussions about divine intervention and human free will. Within the chapter, it is part of God's instruction to Moses about what will happen when he confronts Pharaoh, indicating a pre-ordained outcome for Pharaoh's resistance.

The statement 'I will kill thy son, thy firstborn' is often quoted as a direct threat from God. In its context, it is a specific warning Moses is commanded to deliver to Pharaoh if Pharaoh refuses to let Israel, whom God calls His 'firstborn,' go.
